cityEvents.title: Brutus watches his sons executed
cityEvents.summary: The consul L. Junius Brutus sat on the tribunal while his own sons, caught plotting to restore the Tarquins, were stripped, flogged and beheaded at the stake. Livy stresses that the whole people watched the father's face rather than the punishment.
cityEvents.locName: consular tribunal in the Comitium, at the NW corner of the Forum
cityEvents.note: Legendary tradition. Livy places the punishment at the consuls' tribunal; the Comitium is the conventional site of such public executions.

cityEvents.title: The Tarquins' harvest thrown into the Tiber
cityEvents.summary: The standing grain on the Tarquins' land between city and river was cut and tipped into the Tiber. Livy reports the tradition that the sheaves caught on the shallows and silted into the Tiber Island; the confiscated field became the Campus Martius.
cityEvents.locName: the Tiber Island, said to have formed from the Tarquins' grain
cityEvents.note: Aetiological legend; the island is a natural rock outcrop.

cityEvents.title: Valerius pulls down his house on the Velia
cityEvents.summary: Suspected of aiming at kingship because his house towered over the Forum from the Velia, P. Valerius had it demolished overnight and rebuilt at the foot of the slope. The people repaid him with the name Publicola.
cityEvents.locName: summit of the Velia overlooking the Forum, later site of the Temple of Venus and Roma
cityEvents.note: Later tradition located the house near the Vica Pota shrine at the foot of the Velia.

cityEvents.title: Dedication of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
cityEvents.summary: The consul M. Horatius Pulvillus dedicated the Capitoline temple on the Ides of September, holding the doorpost while his enemies tried to stop him with false news of his son's death. The Ides of September remained the temple's anniversary.
cityEvents.locName: doorway of the cella of the Capitoline temple

cityEvents.title: Horatius Cocles holds the Sublician bridge
cityEvents.summary: When Porsenna's army stormed the Janiculum and drove the Romans to the river, Horatius Cocles held the far end of the wooden Pons Sublicius until it was cut down behind him, then swam back in armour. A statue of him stood in the Comitium.
cityEvents.locName: the Janiculum (west) end of the Pons Sublicius
cityEvents.note: Legend. The exact site of the Pons Sublicius is debated; it lay just below the Pons Aemilius near the Forum Boarium.

cityEvents.title: Mucius Scaevola burns his hand
cityEvents.summary: C. Mucius crossed to Porsenna's camp across the Tiber, killed the king's secretary by mistake and, threatened with fire, thrust his right hand into the altar flames. The land later given to him across the river was called the Mucia Prata.
cityEvents.locName: Etruscan camp across the Tiber below the Janiculum
cityEvents.note: Legend; camp position is a guess.

cityEvents.title: Cloelia's equestrian statue at the top of the Sacra Via
cityEvents.summary: The hostage Cloelia led the girls held by Porsenna across the Tiber under a hail of spears. Rome honoured her with an equestrian statue, the first to a woman, set up at the summit of the Sacra Via.
cityEvents.locName: summit of the Sacra Via on the Velia

cityEvents.title: Temple of Saturn dedicated
cityEvents.summary: The temple at the foot of the Capitol was dedicated on 17 December, the day of the Saturnalia. It held the state treasury (aerarium) for the whole of the Republic.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Saturn, NW end of the Forum

cityEvents.title: Old centurion shows his scars in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: An elderly veteran, enslaved for debt and covered in fresh weals, burst into the Forum and told his story; the crowd rose against the creditors and nearly lynched the senators, starting the crisis that led to the plebs' secession.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum before the Comitium
cityEvents.note: Annalistic tradition.

cityEvents.title: Temple of Mercury dedicated by the centurion Laetorius
cityEvents.summary: The consuls quarrelled over who should dedicate the new temple of Mercury, the merchants' god, facing the Circus Maximus; the people gave the honour to a senior centurion, M. Laetorius, who also founded the merchants' guild. The anniversary fell on the Ides of May.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Mercury on the Aventine side of the Circus Maximus valley

cityEvents.title: Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera dedicated
cityEvents.summary: Sp. Cassius dedicated the temple vowed during a famine, at the foot of the Aventine above the starting gates of the Circus. Built in Tuscan style with terracottas by the Greek artists Damophilus and Gorgasus, it became the headquarters of the plebeian aediles.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Ceres at the NW foot of the Aventine, above the Circus Maximus carceres
cityEvents.note: Exact site not excavated; placed from the ancient descriptions near the carceres.

cityEvents.title: A flogged slave in the Circus and Jupiter's dream
cityEvents.summary: Before the Roman Games a master had a slave driven under the yoke and flogged through the middle of the Circus. Jupiter then appeared in a dream to the plebeian T. Latinius complaining that the 'leading dancer' had displeased him, and the games were repeated.
cityEvents.locName: the arena of the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: House of Spurius Cassius razed; Tellus later built there
cityEvents.summary: Accused of aiming at kingship, the three-times consul Sp. Cassius was condemned; his house was pulled down and the open space in front of the later Temple of Tellus in the Carinae was said to mark the spot.
cityEvents.locName: open area in front of the Temple of Tellus, Carinae
cityEvents.note: The Temple of Tellus (268 BC) stood in the Carinae near the Velia; its exact plan is unknown.

cityEvents.title: Temple of Castor dedicated
cityEvents.summary: A. Postumius' son dedicated the temple vowed at Lake Regillus beside the spring of Juturna, where the Dioscuri had been seen watering their horses after the battle. The Ides of July and the cavalry parade (transvectio equitum) were tied to it.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Castor beside the Lacus Iuturnae, SE side of the Forum

cityEvents.title: Vestal Oppia buried alive
cityEvents.summary: Amid prodigies during the Veientine war, the soothsayers blamed neglected rites; the Vestal Oppia was convicted of unchastity and buried alive at the Colline Gate.
cityEvents.locName: the Campus Sceleratus inside the Colline Gate

cityEvents.title: Temple of Semo Sancus Dius Fidius dedicated on the Quirinal
cityEvents.summary: Sp. Postumius dedicated the temple of the oath god Semo Sancus Dius Fidius on the Quirinal, near the later Porta Sanqualis; it kept the treaty with Gabii written on an ox hide and a bronze statue said to be of Tanaquil.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Semo Sancus on the Quirinal near the Porta Sanqualis

cityEvents.title: Appius Herdonius seizes the Capitol
cityEvents.summary: A Sabine adventurer with some 2500 exiles and slaves landed by night from the Tiber and seized the Capitol and Arx, calling on slaves to rise. The consul P. Valerius retook the citadel with Tusculan help and was killed in the assault.
cityEvents.locName: Capitoline temple precinct and Arx

cityEvents.title: Cincinnatus called from his plough
cityEvents.summary: Envoys found L. Quinctius Cincinnatus digging his four-iugera farm across the Tiber, opposite the later navalia; his wife fetched his toga from the hut and he was hailed dictator. The plot was remembered as the Prata Quinctia.
cityEvents.locName: the Prata Quinctia across the Tiber, opposite the Navalia
cityEvents.note: Livy: 'trans Tiberim, contra eum ipsum locum ubi nunc navalia sunt'. The navalia are themselves disputed (Campus Martius bend or Testaccio); placed opposite the Campus Martius bend.

cityEvents.title: The Twelve Tables set up before the Rostra
cityEvents.summary: The decemvirs' code, the first written Roman law, was engraved on bronze (or wooden) tablets and fixed in public view in the Comitium in front of the speakers' platform; tradition says the Gauls destroyed the originals in 390.
cityEvents.locName: the Comitium, before the old Rostra

cityEvents.title: Verginius kills his daughter by the shrine of Cloacina
cityEvents.summary: When the decemvir Appius Claudius adjudged Verginia a slave so he could have her, her father seized a butcher's knife from a stall by the shrine of Venus Cloacina, at the shops later called the Tabernae Novae, and stabbed her rather than see her dishonoured. The act triggered the second secession.
cityEvents.locName: beside the shrine of Venus Cloacina at the Tabernae Novae, N side of the Forum in front of the later Basilica Aemilia
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
cityEvents.note: Livy names the spot precisely: 'prope Cloacinae ad tabernas, quibus nunc Novis est nomen'. The round base of the Cloacina shrine survives in front of the Basilica Aemilia.

cityEvents.title: Second secession of the plebs to the Aventine
cityEvents.summary: After Verginia's death the army mutinied and the plebs withdrew in arms first to the Aventine, then to the Mons Sacer, until the decemvirs resigned and the tribunate was restored. The Aventine became the plebs' hill par excellence.
cityEvents.locName: the Aventine hill

cityEvents.title: Spurius Maelius killed; the Aequimaelium
cityEvents.summary: The rich grain dealer Sp. Maelius, accused of buying popularity during famine, was cut down by the master of horse C. Servilius Ahala. His house below the Capitol was razed and the empty plot was called the Aequimaelium.
cityEvents.locName: the Aequimaelium on the Vicus Iugarius below the Capitol
cityEvents.note: The Aequimaelium is attested near the Vicus Iugarius at the SE foot of the Capitol (Liv 24.47.15).

cityEvents.title: Temple of Apollo Medicus dedicated in the Prata Flaminia
cityEvents.summary: The consul Cn. Iulius dedicated the temple vowed during the plague of 433, in the Flaminian meadows outside the Porta Carmentalis. Its later rebuilding by C. Sosius gave it the name Apollo Sosianus.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Apollo, Prata Flaminia beside the later Theatre of Marcellus

cityEvents.title: Juno of Veii carried to the Aventine
cityEvents.summary: After the fall of Veii young men in white asked the cult statue of Juno Regina whether she wished to go to Rome; she was said to nod assent. Camillus vowed her a temple on the Aventine, dedicated in 392.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine

cityEvents.title: A voice on the Nova Via warns of the Gauls
cityEvents.summary: The plebeian M. Caedicius heard in the silence of the night, on the Nova Via above the temple of Vesta, a voice louder than human telling him to warn the magistrates that the Gauls were coming. Ignored, the warning was atoned for after the sack with an altar to Aius Locutius, 'the Speaker'.
cityEvents.locName: the Nova Via above the Temple of Vesta, below the Palatine
cityEvents.note: Livy: 'in Nova Via, ubi nunc sacellum est supra aedem Vestae'.

cityEvents.title: Gaius Fabius Dorsuo walks through the Gallic lines
cityEvents.summary: During the siege of the Capitol, C. Fabius Dorsuo came down in ritual dress carrying the sacred vessels, walked through the Gallic pickets to perform his clan's sacrifice on the Quirinal, and returned unharmed.
cityEvents.locName: the Quirinal, at the Fabian family cult site

cityEvents.title: The geese of Juno wake Manlius on the Arx
cityEvents.summary: Gauls climbed by night up the cliff near the shrine of Carmentis. The dogs stayed silent but the sacred geese of Juno, spared despite the famine, cackled; M. Manlius woke, threw the first Gaul off the summit and saved the citadel.
cityEvents.locName: the Arx, at the sanctuary of Juno where the sacred geese were kept (later Temple of Juno Moneta)
cityEvents.note: Legend. The climb was 'ad Carmentis', near the Porta Carmentalis on the SW side; the geese were on the Arx where Juno Moneta was later built (344).

cityEvents.title: 'Vae victis': the gold weighed in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: When the defenders agreed to pay a thousand pounds of gold, the Gauls used false weights and Brennus threw his sword on the scale with the words 'woe to the conquered'. Tradition says Camillus arrived at that moment and refused the payment.
cityEvents.locName: the Comitium / Forum below the Capitol

cityEvents.title: The Busta Gallica: bodies of the Gauls burned
cityEvents.summary: The Gauls who died of disease in the summer of the siege were heaped up and burned in a low place in the city, which kept the name Busta Gallica, 'the Gallic pyres'.
cityEvents.locName: the Busta Gallica, a low area near the Forum (site uncertain)
cityEvents.note: Varro lists the Busta Gallica with the Doliola and Aequimaelium; probably in the valley below the Capitol.

cityEvents.title: Sacred objects buried in jars: the Doliola
cityEvents.summary: Before the Gauls arrived the flamen Quirinalis and the Vestals buried those sacred objects they could not carry away in small jars beside the flamen's house near the Cloaca Maxima. The spot, the Doliola, was afterwards taboo for spitting.
cityEvents.locName: the Doliola beside the Cloaca Maxima, Velabrum / Forum Boarium

cityEvents.title: Lucius Albinius gives his cart to the Vestals
cityEvents.summary: Climbing the Janiculum road with the rest of the fleeing crowd, the plebeian L. Albinius saw the Vestals on foot with the sacred objects, put his wife and children out of his wagon and drove the priestesses to Caere.
cityEvents.locName: the road up the Janiculum beyond the Sublician bridge

cityEvents.title: The Gauls enter Rome by the Colline Gate
cityEvents.summary: Three days after the Allia the Gauls found the Colline Gate open and the walls unguarded. They marched down to the Forum, where the old ex-magistrates sat waiting in their robes of office in the atria of their houses.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Collina at the N end of the Quirinal
cityEvents.note: Livy says the Gauls entered 'porta Collina'. The Servian wall in stone postdates the sack; gate position is that of the later Porta Collina.

cityEvents.title: Marcus Papirius and the Gaul
cityEvents.summary: A Gaul stroked the beard of the ex-consul M. Papirius, who sat motionless in his curule chair in his atrium; Papirius struck him with his ivory staff and was killed, and the massacre of the old men began.
cityEvents.locName: atria of the nobles' houses around the Forum

cityEvents.title: Hasty rebuilding of the burned city
cityEvents.summary: Rejecting a move to Veii, the Romans rebuilt in a year, taking stone and timber where they liked; Livy explains the crooked streets and the sewers running under houses by this haste.
cityEvents.locName: the whole city around the Forum

cityEvents.title: Trial of Manlius in the Lucus Petelinus
cityEvents.summary: Prosecuted for aiming at kingship, Manlius kept pointing to the Capitol he had saved; the tribunes moved the assembly to the Petelian grove outside the Porta Flumentana, from where the Capitol could not be seen, and he was condemned.
cityEvents.locName: the Lucus Petelinus outside the Porta Flumentana, by the Tiber
cityEvents.note: Grove placed just outside the gate in the low ground of the Campus near the river.

cityEvents.title: Manlius Capitolinus thrown from the Tarpeian Rock
cityEvents.summary: The man who had saved the Capitol from the Gauls was hurled from the cliff of the same hill. His house on the Arx was razed and the gens Manlia forbade its members the name Marcus; the Temple of Juno Moneta later rose on the site.
cityEvents.locName: the Tarpeian Rock, S cliff of the Capitol
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
cityEvents.note: The Rock's exact location is disputed (S face above the Vicus Iugarius / Forum Holitorium vs. the SE corner above the Forum).

cityEvents.title: Camillus vows a temple of Concord
cityEvents.summary: As the struggle over the Licinian-Sextian laws threatened civil war, the old dictator Camillus vowed a temple to Concord if the orders were reconciled; the first plebeian consul followed.
cityEvents.locName: the site of the Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol

cityEvents.title: First stage plays brought in against plague
cityEvents.summary: With plague raging and no human remedy, Etruscan dancers were brought in to perform to the pipe; Livy dates the beginning of Roman drama to this attempt to placate the gods. The performances were held in the Circus valley.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus Maximus valley

cityEvents.title: Dictator drives the nail in the Capitoline temple
cityEvents.summary: To end a plague the elders recalled that a nail had once been driven into the wall of Jupiter's temple, on the side of Minerva's chapel, to mark the year; L. Manlius Imperiosus was named dictator just to drive it.
cityEvents.locName: right wall of the Capitoline temple, by the cella of Minerva

cityEvents.title: Marcus Curtius rides into the chasm
cityEvents.summary: A chasm opened in the middle of the Forum and the seers said it would close only when Rome's chief strength was thrown in. The young knight M. Curtius rode in fully armed; the pit closed over him and the pool that remained was the Lacus Curtius.
cityEvents.locName: the Lacus Curtius, paved enclosure in the centre of the Forum
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
cityEvents.note: One of three aetiologies of the Lacus Curtius (others: the Sabine Mettius Curtius; the consul C. Curtius of 445 who fenced a lightning-struck spot). The paved, fenced area survives.

cityEvents.title: Temple of Juno Moneta dedicated on the Arx
cityEvents.summary: L. Furius Camillus dedicated the temple vowed against the Aurunci on the site of Manlius' razed house. Later the Roman mint worked beside it, which is why money is 'moneta'.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx

cityEvents.title: Ship beaks of Antium fixed to the speakers' platform
cityEvents.summary: After the capture of the Antiate fleet some ships were burned and their bronze beaks (rostra) were fixed to the platform on the edge of the Comitium, which gave the Rostra its name. C. Maenius' column stood nearby.
cityEvents.locName: the old Rostra on the S edge of the Comitium
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

cityEvents.title: Aqua Appia reaches the city at the Porta Trigemina
cityEvents.summary: The censor Appius Claudius brought Rome's first aqueduct underground from the east, to end at the Salinae by the Porta Trigemina, and began the Via Appia from the Porta Capena.
cityEvents.locName: terminal of the Aqua Appia near the Porta Trigemina, Forum Boarium

cityEvents.title: Gnaeus Flavius' bronze shrine of Concord on the Volcanal
cityEvents.summary: The freedman's son and aedile Cn. Flavius, who had published the legal formulas and calendar on whitened boards around the Forum, dedicated a small bronze shrine of Concord in the Graecostasis on the Volcanal against the will of the nobles.
cityEvents.locName: the Area Volcani / Graecostasis beside the Comitium

cityEvents.title: The Ogulnii set up the she-wolf and twins
cityEvents.summary: With fines collected from moneylenders the aediles Cn. and Q. Ogulnius placed a statue group of the twins suckled by the wolf beside the Ficus Ruminalis at the Lupercal, and a bronze quadriga on the roof of Jupiter's temple.
cityEvents.locName: the Ficus Ruminalis by the Lupercal, SW foot of the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Verginia founds the shrine of Plebeian Chastity
cityEvents.summary: Excluded from the patrician shrine of Pudicitia in the Forum Boarium because she had married a plebeian, the patrician Verginia set apart part of her house on the Vicus Longus as an altar for plebeian matrons.
cityEvents.locName: her house on the Vicus Longus (valley between Quirinal and Viminal)

cityEvents.title: First sundial set up at the Temple of Quirinus
cityEvents.summary: L. Papirius Cursor dedicated the Temple of Quirinus vowed by his father and, according to Pliny's source, set up the first sundial in Rome there.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Quirinus on the Quirinal

cityEvents.title: The snake of Aesculapius swims to the Tiber Island
cityEvents.summary: Envoys brought back from Epidaurus a sacred snake embodying the healing god. As the ship came up the Tiber it slipped overboard and swam to the island, where the temple of Aesculapius was then built; the island was later dressed in travertine as a ship.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Aesculapius at the downstream end of the Tiber Island

cityEvents.title: Last secession of the plebs, to the Janiculum
cityEvents.summary: Over debts the plebs seceded for the last time, to the Janiculum; the dictator Q. Hortensius ended it with the law making the decisions of the plebeian assembly binding on all.
cityEvents.locName: the Janiculum

cityEvents.title: Blind Appius Claudius carried into the Curia
cityEvents.summary: When the senate was inclined to accept Pyrrhus' peace offered by his envoy Cineas, the old, blind Appius Claudius had himself carried into the senate house and shamed the senators into refusing to treat while Pyrrhus remained in Italy. Cineas reported that the senate was an assembly of kings.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia Hostilia

cityEvents.title: First gladiatorial show, in the Forum Boarium
cityEvents.summary: Decimus and Marcus Brutus Pera honoured their dead father with three pairs of gladiators fighting in the cattle market. Gladiators would later move to the Forum and, centuries later, to the amphitheatres.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum Boarium

cityEvents.title: Sundial from Catana set up by the Rostra
cityEvents.summary: M'. Valerius Messalla brought a sundial from captured Catana and set it on a column beside the Rostra. It was 4 degrees wrong for Rome, but Romans told the time by it for 99 years.
cityEvents.locName: on a column beside the old Rostra

cityEvents.title: Column of Duilius raised at the Rostra
cityEvents.summary: After the naval victory at Mylae, Duilius was honoured with a column decorated with ship beaks near the Rostra, and allowed a torch-bearer and piper to escort him home from dinner.
cityEvents.locName: Columna rostrata near the Rostra / Volcanal

cityEvents.title: Claudia wishes her brother would lose another fleet
cityEvents.summary: Jostled by the crowd as she left the games, Claudia, sister of the admiral who had thrown the sacred chickens overboard and lost the fleet at Drepana, said she wished her brother were alive to lose another fleet and thin out the mob. The aediles fined her.
cityEvents.locName: leaving the games (Circus Maximus)

cityEvents.title: Metellus rescues the Palladium from the burning Temple of Vesta
cityEvents.summary: When the temple of Vesta caught fire the pontifex maximus L. Caecilius Metellus ran into the shrine, which no man might enter, and carried out the Palladium; he lost his sight and was granted the right to ride to the senate in a carriage.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Vesta

cityEvents.title: First Latin play staged at the Ludi Romani
cityEvents.summary: At the Roman Games of 240 the Greek freedman Livius Andronicus staged the first scripted play in Latin, a translation from Greek. Performances were in temporary wooden stands near the Circus.
cityEvents.locName: temporary stage at the Ludi Romani, Circus Maximus valley

cityEvents.title: Temple of Janus closed for the first time since Numa
cityEvents.summary: After the First Punic War the consul T. Manlius Torquatus closed the doors of the Ianus Geminus at the Argiletum, the sign that Rome was at peace, for the first time since King Numa. They were open again within a few years.
cityEvents.locName: the Ianus Geminus at the Forum end of the Argiletum

cityEvents.title: Gauls and Greeks buried alive in the Forum Boarium
cityEvents.summary: On orders from the Sibylline books, a Gallic man and woman and a Greek man and woman were buried alive in a stone chamber in the cattle market, a rite repeated in 216 and 114/113.
cityEvents.locName: an underground chamber in the Forum Boarium

cityEvents.title: Gaius Flaminius lays out the Circus Flaminius
cityEvents.summary: As censor, C. Flaminius built the Via Flaminia and laid out the Circus Flaminius in the Prata Flaminia, an open arena for assemblies, markets and the Taurian games.
cityEvents.locName: Circus Flaminius in the southern Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: 'We have been beaten in a great battle'
cityEvents.summary: News of Trasimene brought crowds to the Comitium and the Curia; toward sunset the praetor M. Pomponius announced from the Rostra: 'pugna magna victi sumus'. Women waited at the gates for news of their men.
cityEvents.locName: Comitium before the Curia; announcement from the Rostra

cityEvents.title: Saturnalia celebrated with a public banquet
cityEvents.summary: After Trasimene the Saturnalia were renewed with a sacrifice at the Temple of Saturn, a lectisternium arranged by senators and a public banquet, and the cry 'Io Saturnalia' resounded through the city day and night.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Saturn

cityEvents.title: Vestals Opimia and Floronia condemned after Cannae
cityEvents.summary: Amid the panic after Cannae two Vestals were convicted of unchastity: one was buried alive at the Colline Gate, the other killed herself; the scribe who had seduced one was beaten to death in the Comitium. Gauls and Greeks were again buried alive in the Forum Boarium.
cityEvents.locName: the Campus Sceleratus inside the Colline Gate
cityEvents.note: The Campus Sceleratus lay inside the Servian wall just right of the road at the Porta Collina (Liv 8.15.8).

cityEvents.title: Fire from the Salinae to the Porta Carmentalis
cityEvents.summary: A fire burned for two nights and a day, levelling everything between the salt stores and the Porta Carmentalis, including the Aequimaelium, the Vicus Iugarius and the temples of Fortuna, Mater Matuta and Spes outside the gate.
cityEvents.locName: between the Salinae and the Porta Carmentalis, around the twin temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta (Sant'Omobono)

cityEvents.title: Hannibal rides up to the Colline Gate
cityEvents.summary: Marching on Rome to draw the army from Capua, Hannibal camped by the Anio and rode with 2000 horsemen to the temple of Hercules outside the Colline Gate to inspect the walls. Romans later boasted the land of his camp sold at full price during the siege.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Hercules outside the Porta Collina

cityEvents.title: Arson in the Forum on the Quinquatrus
cityEvents.summary: On the night before the Quinquatrus fires broke out at several points: the Seven Shops, the fish market, the Atrium Regium and the shops around the Lautumiae burned, and the Temple of Vesta was saved by thirteen slaves, who were freed. Campanian nobles were convicted of arson.
cityEvents.locName: the N side of the Forum: Septem Tabernae, Forum Piscarium, Atrium Regium

cityEvents.title: Twenty-seven girls sing Livius' hymn through the streets
cityEvents.summary: To expiate prodigies, a procession led by two white heifers and 27 maidens singing a hymn by Livius Andronicus went from the Temple of Apollo through the Porta Carmentalis and the Vicus Iugarius into the Forum, then by the Vicus Tuscus and the Velabrum through the Forum Boarium to the temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine.
cityEvents.locName: route: Porta Carmentalis, Vicus Iugarius, Forum, Vicus Tuscus, Velabrum, Forum Boarium, Aventine

cityEvents.title: The fire of Vesta goes out
cityEvents.summary: The eternal fire in the Temple of Vesta was found extinguished through the negligence of a Vestal; she was scourged by the pontifex maximus and a day of supplication was decreed.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Vesta

cityEvents.title: The Great Mother brought to the Palatine
cityEvents.summary: The black meteorite of Cybele from Pessinus, received at Ostia by P. Scipio Nasica, was passed hand to hand by the leading matrons to the city and placed in the Temple of Victoria on the Palatine on 4 April, the first day of the Megalesia.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Victoria on the Palatine (later beside the Temple of Magna Mater)

cityEvents.title: Triumph of Scipio Africanus
cityEvents.summary: Scipio returned from Africa to the most splendid triumph yet seen, depositing 123,000 pounds of silver in the treasury in the Temple of Saturn and closing at the Capitol.
cityEvents.locName: the treasury in the Temple of Saturn, on the triumphal route up the Clivus Capitolinus

cityEvents.title: The procession of the Roman Games
cityEvents.summary: Before the races the pompa circensis wound from the Capitol down through the Forum, along the Vicus Tuscus and the Velabrum to the Circus Maximus: the magistrate in triumphal dress, youths on horseback, chariots, athletes, dancers in armour and satyrs, and the images of the gods.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Pompae of the Circus Maximus at the end of the procession
cityEvents.note: Annual; Dionysius follows Fabius Pictor's description of the 3rd-century BC procession.

cityEvents.title: Women fill the streets to repeal the Lex Oppia
cityEvents.summary: When the wartime law limiting women's gold and coloured clothing came up for repeal, matrons blocked every street and approach to the Forum, besieging the doors of the tribunes who opposed it, despite Cato's speech; the law was repealed.
cityEvents.locName: the streets and approaches to the Forum and Capitol

cityEvents.title: Tiber flood brings down buildings at the Porta Flumentana
cityEvents.summary: The Tiber flooded the low-lying parts of the city and several buildings collapsed around the Porta Flumentana, the river gate between Forum Holitorium and Forum Boarium.
cityEvents.locName: around the Porta Flumentana on the river bank

cityEvents.title: Plautus' guide to the Forum: perjurers and braggarts
cityEvents.summary: In the Curculio the stage manager tells the audience where to find every kind of Roman: perjurers in the Comitium, liars and braggarts at the shrine of Cloacina, rich spendthrift husbands under the basilica, and solid rich citizens strolling in the lower Forum.
cityEvents.locName: the Comitium and the shrine of Cloacina
cityEvents.note: Play dated c. 193 BC; the year is approximate.

cityEvents.title: Plautus: moneylenders under the Old Shops, sharpers behind Castor
cityEvents.summary: The same speech sends the audience to the Tabernae Veteres for those who lend and borrow at interest, to the open drain in mid-Forum for show-offs, and behind the Temple of Castor for men 'whom you would be foolish to trust'.
cityEvents.locName: the Tabernae Veteres on the S side of the Forum, and behind the Temple of Castor

cityEvents.title: Plautus: the Vicus Tuscus, where men sell themselves
cityEvents.summary: In the Etruscan street running from the Forum to the Velabrum, says the Curculio, 'are men who sell themselves', a jibe at male prostitutes in the busy commercial street.
cityEvents.locName: the Vicus Tuscus between Forum and Velabrum

cityEvents.title: Plautus: bakers, butchers and soothsayers of the Velabrum
cityEvents.summary: Plautus closes his tour in the Velabrum, the low market quarter under the Palatine, 'where you will find a baker, a butcher or a soothsayer'.
cityEvents.locName: the Velabrum market quarter

cityEvents.title: Flood carries away two bridges
cityEvents.summary: A violent flood of the Tiber destroyed two bridges and many buildings, especially around the Porta Flumentana; a rock-fall from the Capitol onto the Vicus Iugarius killed many people.
cityEvents.locName: Vicus Iugarius below the Capitol, and the Porta Flumentana

cityEvents.title: Fire in the Forum Boarium burns the riverside shops
cityEvents.summary: A fire broke out in the Forum Boarium and for a day and a night the buildings facing the Tiber burned, with all the shops and their costly goods.
cityEvents.locName: riverside buildings of the Forum Boarium

cityEvents.title: An ox climbs to a rooftop in the Carinae
cityEvents.summary: Among the prodigies of 191, an ox in the Carinae climbed the stairs of a building onto its tiled roof. The haruspices ordered it burned alive and its ashes thrown into the Tiber.
cityEvents.locName: a building in the Carinae, between the Velia and the Oppian

cityEvents.title: The Bacchanalia exposed
cityEvents.summary: The freedwoman Hispala Faecenia told the consul Postumius of nocturnal Bacchic rites in the grove of Stimula near the Aventine and the Tiber. The senate's decree led to thousands of arrests and executions across Italy.
cityEvents.locName: the grove of Stimula at the foot of the Aventine by the Tiber
cityEvents.note: Ovid (Fasti 6.503) places the grove of Stimula near the Tiber at the Aventine.

cityEvents.title: Cato builds the Basilica Porcia beside the Curia
cityEvents.summary: As censor, Cato bought two private houses and four shops at the Lautumiae next to the Curia and built Rome's first named basilica, a covered hall for business and the tribunes' bench.
cityEvents.locName: beside the Curia Hostilia at the Lautumiae, NW corner of the Forum

cityEvents.title: The 'books of Numa' burned in the Comitium
cityEvents.summary: Workmen digging on the Janiculum in the field of the scribe L. Petillius found two stone chests inscribed with Numa's name, one empty and one holding Greek and Latin books on religion. The praetor judged them subversive and they were burned in the Comitium by the sacrificial attendants.
cityEvents.locName: a fire in the Comitium; the chests found on the Janiculum

cityEvents.title: Censors build the Basilica Fulvia et Aemilia
cityEvents.summary: The censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior built a basilica behind the new shops (argentariae novae) on the north side of the Forum, the predecessor of the Basilica Aemilia.
cityEvents.locName: N side of the Forum behind the Tabernae Novae

cityEvents.title: Censor strips the marble roof of Juno Lacinia
cityEvents.summary: Q. Fulvius Flaccus took half the marble roof tiles of the temple of Juno at Croton for his new Temple of Fortuna Equestris in Rome. The senate ordered them returned, but no workman could refit them and they lay in the temple court.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Fortuna Equestris near the later Theatre of Pompey

cityEvents.title: Scipio Africanus' house becomes the Basilica Sempronia
cityEvents.summary: The censor Ti. Sempronius Gracchus bought the house of Scipio Africanus behind the Old Shops by the statue of Vortumnus, together with the butchers' stalls and shops, and built the Basilica Sempronia on the site. Caesar's Basilica Julia later replaced it.
cityEvents.locName: behind the Tabernae Veteres near the Vortumnus statue, under the later Basilica Julia

cityEvents.title: Three-day triumph of Aemilius Paullus
cityEvents.summary: For three days spoils of Macedon passed through the decorated city: statues and paintings on 250 wagons, then gold and silver, then the captive King Perseus and his children. Paullus' two young sons had died just before and after the triumph.
cityEvents.locName: the triumphal route along the Sacra Via to the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Carneades argues for and against justice
cityEvents.summary: On the Athenian embassy of philosophers, Carneades spoke one day in praise of justice and the next refuted it, captivating Roman youth; Cato had the senate send the envoys home quickly.
cityEvents.locName: the Graecostasis by the Comitium, where envoys waited (lectures at unknown places)

cityEvents.title: Senate orders the stone theatre demolished
cityEvents.summary: A permanent theatre begun by the censors on the slope from the Lupercal toward the Palatine was torn down on the motion of Scipio Nasica Corculum as harmful to public morals; spectators were made to stand.
cityEvents.locName: slope from the Lupercal up the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Metellus Macedonicus builds the first marble temple
cityEvents.summary: Q. Caecilius Metellus surrounded the temples of Jupiter Stator and Juno Regina in the Campus with a portico and set in front the bronze equestrian group of Alexander's companions at the Granicus by Lysippus; Jupiter Stator was the first marble temple in Rome.
cityEvents.locName: Porticus Metelli (later Porticus Octaviae), southern Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: Tribune turns his back on the Curia to address the Forum
cityEvents.summary: The tribune C. Licinius Crassus, speaking from the Rostra, broke with custom by turning to face the open Forum and the people rather than the Comitium and the senate house, a gesture remembered as transferring power to the people.
cityEvents.locName: the old Rostra, between Comitium and Forum
cityEvents.note: Plutarch (CG 5) attributes the same gesture to Gaius Gracchus.

cityEvents.title: Aqua Marcia brought up to the Capitol
cityEvents.summary: The praetor Q. Marcius Rex built the high-level Aqua Marcia and, against the objection of the decemvirs who consulted the Sibylline books, carried its water up to the Capitol.
cityEvents.locName: the Capitol, terminus of the Aqua Marcia

cityEvents.title: Tribune Octavius deposed and dragged from the Rostra
cityEvents.summary: When his colleague M. Octavius vetoed the land bill, Tiberius Gracchus had the tribes vote him out of office; Octavius was hauled from the Rostra by Gracchus' freedmen, an unprecedented step.
cityEvents.locName: the Rostra and the voting space of the Forum

cityEvents.title: Nasica leads the senators out of the Temple of Fides
cityEvents.summary: The senate met in the Temple of Fides on the Capitol while Gracchus' assembly gathered outside. When the consul refused to act, the pontifex maximus Scipio Nasica pulled his toga over his head and led senators and their clients out, armed with broken benches.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Fides beside the Capitoline temple precinct
cityEvents.note: Fides stood near the Area Capitolina; its plan has not been securely identified.

cityEvents.title: Tiberius Gracchus clubbed to death on the Capitol
cityEvents.summary: Tiberius tripped over bodies as he fled toward the doors of Jupiter's temple and was beaten to death with a bench leg near the statues of the kings; some 300 supporters died. The bodies were thrown into the Tiber by night, the first political bloodshed in the city since the kings.
cityEvents.locName: Area Capitolina, before the doors of the Temple of Jupiter by the statues of the kings
